lead: Every GIS feature carries two kinds of information. Spatial data says where it is: coordinates in a stated system, plus shape, size, orientation and stored neighbour relations. Attribute data says what it is: a table of properties such as type, depth or ward. A key joins the two halves. This split lets a city ask 'which bore wells are deeper than 60 m' and also 'which wells lie inside ward 7'. The same design supports land records, pipeline maintenance, disaster maps and bus route planning.
prereq: You need: the five parts of a GIS from GIS components, and coordinates and map scales.

blocks.text: Spatial data is the where half. It stores a feature's position in a stated coordinate system, such as easting and northing in metres. Easting is distance east of the origin; northing is distance north. Without the stated system and units the numbers mean nothing. Spatial data also stores shape, size and orientation: a point has no length, a line has length, a polygon has area and a perimeter.

The same object can change primitive with scale. A town is a point on a national map and a polygon on a district map. A road is a line at city scale and a polygon in a land acquisition plan. GIS distinguishes continuous fields from discrete objects. Elevation and temperature are fields: a value exists everywhere. Wells and parcels are objects: each has a boundary or a point location.

Topology is the stored set of neighbour relations. Adjacency means two polygons share a boundary. Containment means one feature lies inside another, such as a well inside ward 7. Connectivity means lines meet at nodes, as pipes do in a water network. Topology answers many location questions quickly and helps catch slivers after overlay. The physical storage of geometry is covered in raster and vector models.

Attribute data is the what half. It is a table: each record is one feature and each field is one property. Standard tables have features as rows and fields as columns, as in the figure. Field values follow a measurement scale, which fixes the arithmetic that is valid.

items: Nominal: labels only. Soil type, road class and well type allow equality and counting, not averaging.
Ordinal: ordered labels. Condition rank 1 to 5 allows sorting and a median, but gaps between ranks need not be equal.
Interval: equal gaps, no true zero. Temperature in °C allows addition, subtraction and a mean; 20 °C is not twice 10 °C.
Ratio: equal gaps and a true zero. Depth in m, length in m and population allow all arithmetic and ratios.

blocks.text: A number can still be nominal. Ward 7 is a label, not a quantity; averaging wards 7 and 9 to get 8 is meaningless. Depth 80 m is ratio because 0 m is a real absence of depth and 80 m is twice 40 m. Marking the scale prevents wrong operations before any query is written.

A primary key is a field with a unique value for each record. It links the attribute row to the geometry. A join merges two tables on a shared key. A one-to-one join matches one row to one row; a one-to-many join matches one row to many. A well table can join to a ward boundary table on the ward number. Many wells lie in one ward, so from wells to ward the join is many-to-one. The key must have the same type on both sides: text '07' will not join to numeric 7 until one side is cleaned.

An attribute query tests fields: 'all bore wells deeper than 60 m'. A spatial query tests geometry or location: 'all wells inside ward 7'. Both can run together, but they are different operations. Metadata records source, date, scale, accuracy and owner. A layer without metadata cannot be judged fit for a new use. See spatial analysis and overlay for combining such layers.

Four well points W1 to W4, with W3 and W4 marked as deep. Right: an attribute table of well, easting, type, depth and ward, with depths 80 and 65 highlighted, and the results of the two queries.

examples.question: Four tube wells are surveyed. Well 1: easting 412 m, northing 1330 m, open, depth 40 m. Well 2: 415 m, 1332 m, open, 55 m. Well 3: 418 m, 1328 m, bore, 80 m. Well 4: 421 m, 1331 m, bore, 65 m. Ward 7 is the polygon with easting 400 to 416 m and northing 1320 to 1340 m; ward 9 lies east of it. (a) State the measurement scale of depth and of type. (b) Run the attribute query depth > 60 m. (c) Run the spatial query "inside ward 7" on the coordinates. (d) Store the result as a ward field and name the key and cardinality of a join to the ward boundary table.
steps: (a) Depth has a true zero (0 m means no depth) and equal metre steps, so it is a ratio scale: 80 m is twice 40 m. Type (open, bore) has no order, so it is nominal.
(b) Test the depth field: Well 1, 40 m, false; Well 2, 55 m, false; Well 3, 80 m, true; Well 4, 65 m, true. Wells 3 and 4 pass. No coordinate was used.

(c) Test the geometry: a point is inside the rectangle if 400 ≤ E ≤ 416 and 1320 ≤ N ≤ 1340. Well 1 (412, 1330): inside. Well 2 (415, 1332): inside. Well 3 (418, 1328): E = 418 > 416, outside. Well 4 (421, 1331): outside. Wells 1 and 2 are in ward 7. No attribute was used. (For a ward of any shape the GIS runs a point-in-polygon test instead of the two inequalities.)

(d) Writing the result into each well record gives a ward field: 7, 7, 9, 9. The join key to the ward boundary table is the ward number. Many wells share one ward, so the join from wells to wards is many-to-one.
examples.answer: Depth is ratio and type nominal. The attribute query depth > 60 m returns Wells 3 and 4; the spatial query inside ward 7 returns Wells 1 and 2. The ward number is the key, and the wells-to-ward join is many-to-one.

traps: Calling the easting and northing rows 'attributes'. They are the spatial half; the properties below them are the attribute half.
Joining ward '07' to numeric 7 without converting one side. Join keys must have the same type and a clean value.
Treating ward 7 as a ratio value and averaging ward numbers. Ward is a nominal label, not a quantity.

Mixing an attribute query with a spatial query. "Depth > 60 m" tests a field; "inside ward 7" tests coordinates against a boundary. Once the answer is stored as a ward field, "ward = 7" is an attribute query that copies an earlier spatial result.
Assuming a feature has one fixed primitive. A town or road can be a point, a line or a polygon at different scales.

quiz.q: Define spatial data and attribute data in one line each.
quiz.a: Spatial data: location, shape, size, orientation and topology. Attribute data: properties stored in fields.

quiz.q: Why store topology instead of recomputing neighbours from coordinates every time?
quiz.a: Stored topology makes adjacency, containment and connectivity queries fast and stable, and helps detect slivers after overlay.

quiz.q: Using the worked example, which wells have depth ≥ 70 m, and which lie in ward 9?
quiz.a: Depth ≥ 70 m: Well 3 only (80 m), an attribute query. Ward 9: Wells 3 and 4, whose eastings 418 and 421 m are east of the ward 7 boundary at 416 m, a spatial query.

quiz.q: A town is a point on a national map and a polygon on a district map. Is this an error? Explain.
quiz.a: No. The primitive follows scale and purpose. At national scale the town's internal shape is irrelevant; at district scale it matters.

quiz.q: Classify these queries: 'depth > 60 m' and 'inside ward 7'.
quiz.a: 'Depth > 60 m' is an attribute query. 'Inside ward 7' is a spatial query.

quiz.q: Why will ward value '07' not join to numeric 7, and what fix is needed?
quiz.a: The key types differ. Convert both to the same type, such as integer 7, after checking that no data is lost.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry these two halves live in a spatial database such as PostGIS, where geometry and attributes are queried together by SQL. Data teams spend much time on keys, measurement scales and metadata because wrong joins and mixed units survive silently into dashboards. Open data portals publish layers with licences and update dates, and metadata standards record exactly those fields. Search next for spatial database, GeoJSON, data lineage and metadata catalogue.
